frames.narration: A user picks a 3 MB photo. The app asks the post API for permission to upload. The API creates a post row marked pending and checks the user's limits, but it never touches the photo itself.

messages.label: I want to post a photo, 3 MB

frames.narration: The API answers with a signed URL for one object key, valid for 15 minutes and for a single PUT up to 10 MB. The phone sends the 3 MB straight to object storage, so no application server carries the bytes.

Object storage announces that a new object exists. The event goes onto a queue, so processing can be slow or can fall behind without the upload noticing. The post is still pending, and the user sees their own photo from the phone's local copy.
An image worker takes the job, reads the original and checks that it is a real image of a sane size. It strips the location data and turns the photo upright.

The worker writes 4 sizes (150, 320, 640 and 1080 px) in 2 formats, 8 files of about 0.4 MB in total. Each file's name contains a hash of its content, so a name never changes meaning. Then it marks the post ready. If the job runs twice, it writes the same names with the same bytes.

A follower's phone needs the 640 px version of about 60 KB. The nearest CDN node does not have it yet, so it fetches the file once from object storage, keeps it for a year because the name never changes, and sends it. The next million followers are served by the CDN alone.

The follower double-taps. The API first records the unique (post, user) pair, which rejects a repeat. Then it adds 1 to one of the post's 16 counter shards, chosen at random, so a viral post does not pile its updates onto one row.

The count that readers see is the sum of the 16 shards, cached for a second. It can be a little behind, and the tapping user sees their own like at once on their screen. When the poster later deletes the photo, a purge removes the files and the CDN entries.
